biographies.chicago_connection: Direct: both companies were Chicago firms — Montgomery Ward founded its Chicago mail-order business in 1872; Sears was a Chicago company whose catalogs are held in Smithsonian collections under place 'Chicago, Illinois'.

links.evidence: Smithsonian Institution collection record: 'Trade catalogs from Sears, Roebuck and Co. Inc.', Place: Chicago, Illinois; Location: Trade Literature at the American History Museum Library.
links.uncertainty: The record covers the trade-catalog series rather than one dated issue; no single issue was pulled as the exemplar.
links.value: Sears, Roebuck and Co. mail-order catalogs, held in the Smithsonian Libraries Trade Literature Collections (place: Chicago, Illinois).

links.evidence: Aaron Montgomery Ward founded the Chicago mail-order business in 1872; his first catalog was a single sheet listing 163 items. Sears, Roebuck and Co. was the Chicago competitor founded by Richard Sears.
links.uncertainty: 1872 and the 163-item sheet rest on secondary accounts (including Wikipedia's Aaron Montgomery Ward entry); not corroborated from a primary company record here.
links.value: Aaron Montgomery Ward (founded the Chicago mail-order business in 1872; first catalog a one-sheet of 163 items); Sears, Roebuck and Co., Chicago (Richard Sears).

links.evidence: City of Chicago landmark report on the Sears district: by 1895 the catalog exceeded 500 pages with a vast merchandise range; historian Daniel Boorstin called it 'the Bible of the new rural consumption communities.'
links.uncertainty: Page counts are period claims reported by the landmark study.
links.value: The multi-hundred-page illustrated 'Big Book' — over 500 pages by 1895, covering shoes, garments, wagons, stoves, furniture, musical instruments, firearms, bicycles, and more.

links.evidence: Ward's 1872 founding (secondary); Smithsonian Magazine dates the end of Sears's 'Big Book' to January 25, 1993; a secondary source dates the end of the Montgomery Ward catalog to 1985.
links.uncertainty: 1872 and 1985 endpoints rest on secondary sources; only the 1993 Sears end date is institutionally sourced.
links.value: From Montgomery Ward's 1872 Chicago founding through the Sears 'Big Book' era, which ceased production on January 25, 1993 (the Ward catalog ended in 1985, per secondary sources).

links.evidence: City of Chicago landmark report quotes the 1894 cover declarations 'Book of Bargains: A Money Saver for Everyone' and 'Cheapest Supply House on Earth,' and Sears's motto 'We Can't Afford to Lose a Customer.'
links.uncertainty: Quoted slogans are from the landmark report, not from a retrieved catalog cover image.
links.value: Early Sears catalogs billed themselves as the 'Cheapest Supply House on Earth' and the 'Book of Bargains,' with the motto 'We Can't Afford to Lose a Customer'; Richard Sears wrote nearly all the catalog copy himself until his 1908 retirement.

links.evidence: Historian Einav Rabinovitch-Fox, quoted in Finance & Commerce (2018): buying by mail order 'allowed African-Americans to assert their right to participate as equals in the market, turning the act of shopping via the mail into a political act of resistance.' Louis Hyman's research (reproduced educational PDF) adds that the catalog gave Black Southern families autonomy from discriminatory merchants, that Sears's founders ran photographs to 'prove' they were white, and that merchants burned the catalogs.
links.uncertainty: The Hyman details rest on a reproduced educational PDF whose provenance is weaker than the Finance & Commerce interview — the Verified grade rests on the Rabinovitch-Fox quotation.
links.value: For Black consumers under Jim Crow, ordering by mail was a documented political act: it let African Americans bypass discriminatory stores and 'assert their right to participate as equals in the market.'
links.red_team_note: Mail-order-as-political-act rests on modern historian Rabinovitch-Fox's framing alone; methodology 4.2 caps at Provisional.

links.evidence: The Rabinovitch-Fox quotation above; the Hyman account of catalog ordering giving Black Southern families autonomy; Smithsonian curator Kathleen Franz documents the catalog's secondary household uses (Smithsonian Magazine, 2023-01-25).
links.uncertainty: Specific Black-family order records were not retrieved; the use pattern is documented through historians' accounts.
links.value: Black families, especially in the rural South, ordered goods by mail to avoid discriminatory local merchants; the catalog itself was also re-used around the home.

links.value: No dated photographs of catalog consumer use were located in this pass.

links.evidence: Ward founding (connectingthewindycity/Wikipedia); Sears details (Chicago landmark report; History); Rosenwald-Washington partnership and school figures (Finance & Commerce, 2018).

links.value: Round orange metal tin with black-and-red typography, multilingual directions, a woman's head in profile, and a lid portrait of a man and woman.

links.evidence: NMAAHC (company founded 1925); lid copyright 1926 (primary); tin's barcode text 'www.murrayspomade.com / Established 1925.'
links.uncertainty: The tin's own date is not given; the design era is bounded by the 1926 copyright and the company's continued production.
links.value: From 1925 to the present; the tin design carries a 1926 copyright notice.

links.evidence: The tin itself carries the brand's web-era marketing ('www.MurraysPomade.com', 'Established 1925'); no period print advertisement was retrieved.
links.uncertainty: No period print ad verified; the link rests on the packaging's own marketing text.
links.value: Brand marketing is documented on the packaging itself ('Established 1925'); period print advertising was not located in this pass.

links.evidence: None found — no contemporary documented symbolic meaning for the pomade tin was located; nostalgia for the orange tin is not evidence.
links.uncertainty: Do not treat the tin's iconic status as documented symbolism.
links.value: No documented symbolism located in this pass.

links.evidence: Product copy describes a thick oil/wax pomade for a 'clean, neat look' that 'controls and enhances your natural waves'; Wikipedia notes it was initially marketed toward Black consumers and is notoriously hard to wash out.
links.uncertainty: Commercial product copy and Wikipedia; no primary consumer accounts retrieved.
links.value: Used as a heavy-hold hair dressing for styling and waves; thick oil/wax consistency, famously difficult to wash out.

links.evidence: None found.
links.uncertainty: Product and advertising photography exists but was not verified here.
links.value: No dated photographs of Murray's consumer use were located in this pass.

links.evidence: NMAAHC collection record read directly; on view in the Cultural Expressions gallery; rights: 'No Known Copyright Restrictions.'
links.uncertainty: None for the fact of the holding.
links.value: NMAAHC 2014.261ab (tin of Murray's Superior Hair Dressing Pomade, gift of Marva P. Wiley).

links.evidence: Archived official company history (Murray, Berlin); NMAAHC record (Wiley donor).
links.uncertainty: Murray and Berlin details rest on the company's own archived history.
links.value: C.D. Murray (founder, began production in his Chicago barbershop in 1925); Harry Berlin (pharmacist who purchased the company in 1959); Marva P. Wiley (donor of the NMAAHC tin).

links.evidence: None found.
links.uncertainty: None claimed.
links.value: No movement membership verified in this pass.

biographies.chicago_connection: No Chicago school yearbook verified in this pass; NMAAHC holds a diploma from Chicago's Muhammad University of Islam (related evidence). The 1970 East High 'Grey Eagle' and 1955 Allen 'Yellow Jacket' are the verified exemplars.

links.evidence: NMAAHC collection record: 1955 Allen University 'Yellow Jacket,' published by Taylor Publishing Company, object 2017.99.2, public domain.
links.uncertainty: None for the accessioned yearbook as cataloged.
links.value: 1955 Allen University 'Yellow Jacket' yearbook, NMAAHC object 2017.99.2.

links.evidence: NMAAHC record lists Taylor Publishing Company as publisher of the 1955 Allen yearbook and of the 1970 East High 'Grey Eagle' (2018.15.3).
links.uncertainty: None for the publisher attribution as cataloged.
links.value: Taylor Publishing Company (Dallas, Texas — publisher of both verified exemplars).

links.evidence: NMAAHC descriptions: campus photographs, academic and social-life documentation, school-life photographs with handwritten inscriptions (1970 'Grey Eagle').
links.uncertainty: None for the cataloged contents.
links.value: Bound yearbook with campus and class photographs documenting academic and social life; the 1970 'Grey Eagle' carries handwritten student inscriptions.

links.evidence: NMAAHC records date the exemplars 1955 and 1970.
links.uncertainty: None for the two exemplars' dates.
links.value: 1955 (Allen University 'Yellow Jacket'); 1970 (East High School 'Grey Eagle').

links.evidence: None found for these copies — yearbook advertising pages were not documented.
links.uncertainty: Yearbooks of the era commonly carried local-business ads, but none was verified for these copies.
links.value: No yearbook advertising located in this pass.

links.evidence: NMAAHC frames the yearbooks as documentation of Black institutional and school life; the symbolic reading rests on museum framing rather than contemporary testimony.
links.uncertainty: Symbolic meaning is museum-framed, not contemporary-sourced — hence Provisional.
links.value: The yearbook as archive and affirmation of Black institutional life — a record of schools as community anchors.

links.evidence: NMAAHC documents handwritten inscriptions in the 1970 'Grey Eagle,' evidence of personal keeping and exchange.
links.uncertainty: Use is inferred from the inscriptions — Provisional, not a primary account of use.
links.value: Students kept, inscribed, and exchanged yearbooks as personal and social records.

links.evidence: NMAAHC records note the yearbooks' photographic contents; the yearbook itself is a photographic record.
links.uncertainty: None for the fact that the yearbooks contain dated photographs.
links.value: The yearbooks are themselves dated photographic records of school life (1955 and 1970).

links.evidence: Both NMAAHC collection records read directly.
links.uncertainty: None for the fact of these holdings.
links.value: NMAAHC 2017.99.2 (1955 Allen University 'Yellow Jacket' — public domain); NMAAHC 2018.15.3 (1970 East High School 'Grey Eagle,' Taylor Publishing).

links.evidence: NMAAHC records (Taylor Publishing; East High students' inscriptions).
links.uncertainty: None for the publisher; the inscribers are anonymous students.
links.value: Taylor Publishing Company (publisher); the East High students whose handwritten inscriptions survive in the 1970 'Grey Eagle.'

links.evidence: NMAAHC holds a diploma from Chicago's Muhammad University of Islam (founded 1934), received by Bobby 6X Jones and signed by Elijah Muhammad — documenting the Black independent-schooling tradition in Chicago.
links.uncertainty: The diploma is related evidence, not a movement membership for the yearbook itself — hence Provisional.
links.value: Black independent schooling tradition (cf. Chicago's Muhammad University of Islam, founded 1934).
